lt:L2.01:0.text: A fisherman named Tom worked on a small boat every morning. One day, Tom caught a fish that was absolutely **enormous** — far bigger than any fish he had ever seen before.

lt:L2.01:1.text: It was so large that he could barely lift it into the boat! Tom's friends at the harbor could not believe their eyes.

lt:L2.01:2.text: "That fish is enormous!" they shouted. Tom laughed and said an enormous fish like that would feed the whole street for a week.

lt:L2.01:3.text: He shared it with every family on his road, and everyone had a wonderful dinner that night.

lt:L2.02:0.text: A little cat named Pip was very **curious**. Every single day, Pip wanted to know what was happening on the other side of the garden wall.

lt:L2.02:1.text: One afternoon, Pip's curious nose led her straight into a bush, where she found a family of hedgehogs curled up asleep! Pip was so curious that she gently poked one with her paw.

lt:L2.02:2.text: The hedgehog woke up, uncurled, and gave a tiny, surprised squeak. Pip jumped back, but she was still curious — she sat and watched the hedgehogs for the rest of the afternoon, learning something new about her garden.

lt:L2.03:0.text: Grandpa was usually calm, but one afternoon he got absolutely **furious**. His favorite garden tools had gone missing from the shed, and he was sure someone had taken them without asking.

lt:L2.03:1.text: He searched the whole yard, muttering to himself, getting more and more furious with every empty corner. Then his granddaughter walked out holding the tools.

lt:L2.03:2.text: "I borrowed them to fix my bike, Grandpa — I forgot to tell you!" she said. Grandpa's furious face softened into a small smile.

lt:L2.03:3.text: "Next time," he said, "just tell me first, and I won't have to get furious over nothing."

lt:L2.04:0.text: Little Ana loved puzzles more than anything, but one rainy afternoon she found herself completely **puzzled**. Her grandmother had given her a box with no picture on the lid and no instructions inside — just three hundred loose pieces.

lt:L2.04:1.text: Ana sat there, puzzled, turning pieces over in her hands, unsure where to even begin. She tried the edges first, but she was still puzzled about which piece connected to which.

lt:L2.04:2.text: Finally, her grandmother sat beside her and said, "When you are puzzled, start with the corners — there are only four, and they always fit first." Ana found a corner, then another, and slowly her puzzled frown turned into a grin.

lt:L2.05:0.text: After a full day at the farm, feeding the animals, mending fences, and carrying heavy buckets of water, farmer Iqbal was completely **exhausted**. His arms ached, his legs felt like stone, and he could barely climb the steps to his own porch.

lt:L2.05:1.text: His son offered to finish the last chore, but Iqbal was too exhausted even to explain what needed doing — he just pointed and nodded. He sat down, closed his eyes, and within minutes he was fast asleep in his chair, still wearing his muddy boots.

lt:L2.05:2.text: When he woke an hour later, he felt much better, though still a little exhausted, and very glad his son had taken care of the rest.

lt:L2.06:0.text: Before crossing the busy market road, Aunt Rukhsana was always very **cautious**. She would stop at the edge, look left, then right, then left again, even if the road looked completely empty.

lt:L2.06:1.text: Her nephew used to tease her about being so cautious, saying it took forever just to cross one small street. One evening, though, a bicycle came speeding around the corner at exactly the moment they stepped off the curb — and because Aunt Rukhsana had been cautious and was watching closely, she pulled her nephew back just in time.

lt:L2.06:2.text: After that, her nephew never teased her again. "Better cautious than sorry," she always says, and now he says it too.

lt:L2.07:0.text: When the school bake sale raised more money than anyone expected, the head teacher decided to give every extra rupee to the small clinic down the road. She was **grateful** — truly grateful — for how hard the students had worked, baking and selling from early morning until the last plate was empty.

lt:L2.07:1.text: One student asked why she looked close to tears. "I am just so grateful," she said.

lt:L2.07:2.text: "You worked all day, and now families who could not afford medicine will get help." The students felt proud too, and decided that being the reason someone else got help was better than any prize. They planned an even bigger, more grateful bake sale for next year.

lt:L2.08:0.text: A young dog named Bruno was usually eager to try anything new, but the first time his owner brought out a bicycle, Bruno was strangely **reluctant**. He backed away, tail low, refusing to go anywhere near the strange spinning wheels.

lt:L2.08:1.text: His owner tried treats, gentle words, even a favorite toy — but Bruno stayed reluctant, watching from a safe distance. Then one afternoon, the owner simply sat beside the bicycle and let Bruno sniff it in his own time, with no pushing at all.

lt:L2.08:2.text: Slowly, Bruno's reluctant ears perked up, and he stepped closer. By the end of the week, the once-reluctant Bruno was trotting happily alongside the bicycle on every walk.

lt:L2.09:0.text: When the class hamster went missing from its cage on a Friday afternoon, every student was **delighted** to hear it had been found safe behind the bookshelf on Monday morning. The teacher was delighted too, and let the whole class take turns holding it gently, one by one.

lt:L2.09:1.text: One boy, who had been especially worried all weekend, was so delighted that he asked if he could bring the hamster home just for one night, to make sure it was really okay. His teacher smiled at how delighted — and relieved — he looked, and said yes, as long as his parents agreed.

lt:L2.09:2.text: That evening, the whole family took turns being delighted by the tiny hamster running on its wheel.

lt:L2.10:0.text: Uncle Hamid had asked his nephew, Bilal, to water the plants every single day while he was away — just that one job. When Hamid came home a week later and found every plant wilted and brown, he was **stubborn** about not letting it go.

lt:L2.10:1.text: "It's just water, once a day," he said, again and again, refusing to accept Bilal's excuses about being busy with exams. Bilal, just as stubborn, insisted exams mattered more than plants.

lt:L2.10:2.text: Neither would budge for two whole days. Finally, Hamid's wife stepped in and pointed out that both of them were being equally stubborn over something they could fix together in ten minutes.

lt:L2.10:3.text: They laughed, apologized, and replanted the garden side by side that weekend.

lt:L2.11:0.text: The night before her first big exam, Ayesha felt more **anxious** than she had ever felt before. Her stomach fluttered, her hands felt cold, and she kept checking the clock, worried she was somehow forgetting something important.

lt:L2.11:1.text: Her older sister noticed how anxious she looked and sat down beside her. "Being a little anxious means you care," her sister said, "but let's make a short plan so the anxious feeling has less to hold onto." Together they wrote down exactly what Ayesha needed for the morning, checked it twice, and set two alarms.

lt:L2.11:2.text: Ayesha still felt a bit anxious as she fell asleep, but far less than before — and in the morning, she walked into the exam room calm and ready.

lt:L2.12:0.text: A wealthy trader in the old bazaar was known across the whole street for being unusually **generous**. Every evening, before he closed his stall, he would give away whatever fruit and bread had not sold that day — never selling it cheap at the last minute, always simply giving it to whoever needed it most.

lt:L2.12:1.text: His neighbors thought he must be losing money, but the trader just smiled and said being generous had brought him more good luck and more loyal customers than any clever deal ever had. One winter, when his own stall caught fire, every single family he had once helped showed up the next morning with tools, wood, and cash to help him rebuild — proof, he said, that generous kindness always finds its way back.

lt:L2.13:0.text: Retrieval passage: A stubborn old goat named Bella refused to leave the muddy field even when it started to rain hard. Her owner, cautious as always, did not want to drag a furious, wet goat across a slippery yard, so he waited, patient, under the barn roof.

lt:L2.13:1.text: After an hour of stubborn standing in the rain, Bella finally got cold enough to trot inside on her own — no longer stubborn, just cautious about getting even wetter. Her owner laughed, dried her off, and said a stubborn goat always changes its mind eventually, as long as you stay cautious and let it happen in its own time.

lt:L3.01:0.text: A long time ago, people who wanted to send a message far away used pigeons. A trained pigeon could find its way home from a hundred miles off.

lt:L3.01:1.text: Today we call sending a fast, important message 'urgent' — it means it cannot wait.

lt:L3.02:0.text: Before bikes had rubber tires, riders used wheels with iron rims. Every bump in the road shook the whole bike — people called it a 'bone-shaker.' A ride that should have felt smooth instead felt rough and tiring.

lt:L3.03:0.text: Mules are often used on farms because they are known to be very sturdy. A mule can carry a heavy load over rough ground for a long time without tiring, which makes it a reliable partner for farm work.

lt:L3.04:0.text: A shopkeeper's closing routine matters because a rushed close can leave a door unlocked or cash uncounted. A careful routine, done the same way every night, reduces the chance of a costly mistake.

lt:L3.05:0.text: Engineers who design robots must consider every possible task the machine will face, because a robot cannot adapt on its own the way a person can. A well-designed robot follows a precise set of instructions, and even a small gap in those instructions can cause a big mistake.

lt:L3.06:0.text: A customer who takes the time to leave a kind note is showing genuine gratitude — a real, felt thanks, not just a quick 'thanks' said out of habit. Genuine gratitude tends to stick with a person much longer than a routine thank-you.

lt:L3.07:0.text: Engineers who inspect a bridge look for tiny cracks long before the bridge is actually in danger of failing. Catching a problem early, while it is still minor, is far cheaper and safer than waiting until it becomes a crisis.

lt:L3.08:0.text: Farmers markets let shoppers buy food directly from the people who grew it, which often means the produce is fresher than what has traveled a long distance to a big store. Buying this way also supports the local economy.

lt:L3.09:0.text: Before horses could be domesticated for riding, humans had to build a relationship of trust with an animal that is naturally alert to danger. A horse that trusts its rider will respond calmly even in a busy, noisy place.

lt:L3.10:0.text: When trains are delayed during heavy rain, it is often because water can seep into the electrical system that controls the tracks, forcing a temporary shutdown until it is safe again.

lt:L3.11:0.text: Communities that organize regular street clean-ups tend to build a stronger sense of civic pride, because neighbors who work side by side start to feel a shared responsibility for the place they live.

lt:L3.12:0.text: Traffic engineers study patterns in road congestion to figure out which streets need a second lane or a new signal. A small change, like a longer green light, can noticeably ease a slow commute for thousands of people.

lt:L3.13:0.text: Talking through a big decision with someone you trust often reveals a perspective you had not considered on your own. A friend can point out a risk or an option you were too close to the problem to notice.

lt:L3.14:0.text: Choosing an outfit for an important meeting is about more than looking neat — it can genuinely affect how confident a person feels walking into the room, which in turn can affect how well they perform.

lt:L3.15:0.text: Reading fiction before bed has been shown to help some people unwind, because following a story shifts attention away from the day's worries and toward a different, absorbing world.

lt:L3.16:0.text: When a whole industry changes quickly, many workers must adapt by learning a new skill, which can feel daunting at first but often opens up options a person had not considered before.

lt:L3.17:0.text: People often find that a day spent helping others, even a small task like a neighborhood clean-up, brings a deeper sense of satisfaction than a day spent purely on entertainment. Researchers call this the difference between pleasure and genuine fulfillment.

lt:L4.01:0.text: Long ago, before streetlights, farmers and travelers used the stars to find their way home. A bright, easy-to-spot group of stars is called a constellation.

lt:L4.02:0.text: Long before cars, people used horses to travel. A caravan was a group of travelers — often with camels or horses — who journeyed together across long, hard roads for safety.

lt:L4.03:0.text: People who care for the sick and injured, easing pain and helping bodies heal, often say the work feels like a calling — something they feel deeply pulled to do, not just a job.

lt:L4.04:0.text: In many places, wild animals like deer must be cautious around people, even kind ones, because their bodies are built to sense danger first and think later.

lt:L4.05:0.text: When people work well together and things go smoothly, we sometimes say the day felt harmonious — everything and everyone fitting together without friction.

lt:L4.06:0.text: When many strangers stay calm together during a problem, like a power cut or a delay, we can say the group showed resilience — the ability to handle a hard moment without falling apart.

lt:L4.07:0.text: In a busy public space, staff are trained to stay composed — calm and in control of their actions and voice — even when something unexpected happens, because panic spreads fast in a crowd.

lt:L4.08:0.text: When someone stays calm and keeps making good choices even after something goes wrong, we can say they showed composure — a steady, level-headed response instead of panic.

lt:L4.09:0.text: A doctor or nurse who stays warm and patient with every person they see, even on an exhausting day, shows real compassion — caring about someone else's pain as if it were your own.

lt:L4.10:0.text: A worker who checks their own work carefully before calling a job finished shows diligence — steady, careful effort, even on small details other people might not notice.

lt:L4.11:0.text: A good doctor, teacher, or guide often shows attentiveness — noticing small details about a person or a situation that someone in a hurry might miss.

lt:L4.12:0.text: Some people believe small signs from nature — a bird building a nest, a certain season's first rain — carry meaning. Scientists call this kind of belief folklore: traditional stories and beliefs passed down between people, not proven by evidence but often carrying real wisdom about nature.

lt:L4.13:0.text: People who keep working toward a goal, even slowly and through setbacks, show perseverance — refusing to give up, even when progress feels slow.

lt:L4.14:0.text: When someone works through a problem methodically instead of guessing, checking each possible cause one at a time, we call that troubleshooting — a careful, step-by-step way of finding and fixing what's wrong.

lt:L4.15:0.text: A notice, a recipe, and a news report are three examples of functional text — writing whose main job is to help you do something (know when the water's off, cook a meal, understand a local event) rather than to tell a story.

read:L2.13:A:0.text: Min and Dad go to visit a friend. / They pack a backpack with a napkin / and a muffin. / "I want to bring the pink rabbit," / Min says, / "because it is fun." / Min and the friend run and jump in the grass. / When they get to the pond, / they sit still. / A fish splashes, / and Min spots an insect on a twig. / The friend is helping Min hunt for bugs. / "Should we catch it?" / the friend asks. / "No, / let's just watch it," / Min says, / "because it is not bad." / They pack up at sunset, / and hug the friend. / Min and Dad go back, / glad and full, / and plan to come again.

read:L2.13:B:0.text: Sam has a shift with a friend from a shop, / helping fix a big backlog of dents and checks. / "This job is a lot, / but his friend can help," / Sam says, / "because two friends finish fast." / They pack the kit, / check the list, / and split the job up. / Sam's friend fixes the dents, / and Sam checks the vans / and prints the list. / At dusk, / the shop has a full stock of fixed vans / and a strong stack of finished checks. / "We should do this again," / Sam's friend says. / "Yes, / because it went fast and we still got it done," / Sam says, / and they clap hands, / glad and calm.

read:L3.01:A:0.text: Jane and Kate are at the lake. / Jane has a cane. / Kate has a cape. / They skate on the lake. / Once, Kate got a cramp. / Jane came and gave Kate a hand. / Kate said, "Thank you, Jane!" / They made a plan to skate again.

read:L3.01:B:0.text: Jake has a case to take to the bank. / He made a plane trip. / At the gate, he got a snack and a cake. / Jake's plane was late, but he was not sad. / He said, "I have cash." / Jake sat and had a nap. / Once the plane came, he got on fast.

read:L3.02:A:0.text: Mike has a bike. / He likes to ride it. / Mike and his dog Spike go for a ride. / Once, Mike's bike went flat. / Mike did not stop. / He got off and did a quick fix. / Spike sat still. / "Only a bit," said Mike, and they went back.

read:L3.02:B:0.text: Kate got a bike to save time. / She rides it to her job many times. / At nine, she locks the bike and clocks in. / Once, the bike would not go, and Kate had to get off and push it. / She was not glad, but she did not quit. / Only a quick fix did it, and the next ride was fine.

read:L3.03:A:0.text: Steve moved to a home. / It is big, and it has a gate. / Steve rode his bike home and did a jig. / He is very glad. / At home, Steve has a cute pet mule named Duke. / Duke likes a plate of grass. / "This home is very fine," said Steve, and he made a note to tell his pal.

read:L3.03:B:0.text: Steve got home very late from his shift. / His job is to help sick kids, and the shift ran long. / At home, he made a snack and sat next to the stove. / His wife left a note: "I made a plate for you." / Steve smiled. / It was a very long shift, but home felt like a rest at last.

read:L3.04:A:0.text: Sam is making a kite. / He is using tape and a stick. / Every bit has to be just so. / Sam is smiling at his plan. / Once it is done, Sam is hoping for a fine time. / He is saving his kite for the big game. / "I made this alone," said Sam, very glad.

read:L3.04:B:0.text: At the end of every shift, Kate is closing the shop at nine. / She is checking the till and saving the cash. / Once the till is closed, she is locking every gate. / Kate is not rushing — she likes taking her time. / "I am making it safe," she said, smiling at her plan for a safe close.

read:L3.05:A:0.text: We go to spot a tiger. / The tiger is silent as it moves. / Because he had a project, a pupil at his class made a robot tiger. / It has one eye that shines. / "This is a great robot!" said the pupil. / We are so glad we came. / We go home and hum a tune, glad for the tigers.

read:L3.05:B:0.text: Kate got a spot in a great program at her job site. / Because there were big tasks, she and the others made a robot to help. / The program runs a set of steps, silent and fast, no fuss. / "We tested it with one eye on the clock," said Kate. / The robot has done every task well. / Kate is glad she got to do this.

read:L3.06:A:0.text: My puppy is very busy. / He runs and hops in the sun by the shed. / My puppy is funny — when he digs in the mud, he gets sticky and muddy. / "Silly puppy!" I said, and gave him a rub. / We go home, and my puppy is happy because he is with me.

read:L3.06:B:0.text: My shift was very busy, because I ran from the front to the back and did not stop by lunch. / When I got back, there was a note from a happy person: "Thank you, you made me very glad." / I am busy, but I am glad I had a busy, happy shift.

read:L3.07:A:0.text: In the city, there is a big bridge. / Many people cross it often. / Once, my class went on a trip to visit it, because it is huge and made of stage-like steps. / When we got to the edge, we could spot a huge cage with a pet inside. / "So nice!" said the people, very glad. / We had a fine time at the bridge.

read:L3.07:B:0.text: Since the bridge in the city closed, many people had to change the plan. / Many people came to fix it, page by page of a plan they had made. / "It is a huge job, but it is not a bad job if we take the time to do it well," said the judge. / People are glad the bridge will be fine once it is fixed.

read:L3.08:A:0.text: Sam and his mom go to the farm. / A big, red barn is at the farm. / Sam pets a cute pup and a fat pig. / "A big cart!" said Sam. / He rides in the cart with his mom, because he likes it a lot. / They spot a hen in the yard. / Once they are done, they have a snack of grapes. / Sam has a whole, fine time at the farm.

read:L3.08:B:0.text: Kate got a job at the market. / She helps at a cart that sells fresh grapes and plums. / At nine, she sets up the cart and starts her shift. / "This job is hard, but I like it," said Kate. / She helps many people at the market, because she likes to help. / Once her shift is done, Kate has a snack and a cup of milk. / She has a whole, fine time at the market.

read:L3.09:A:0.text: At the farm, Sam spots a horse. / The horse has a short, dark mane. / "Can I ride the horse?" asked Sam. / "Yes, hold on well," said his mom. / Sam gets on, and the horse trots because he holds on well. / Sam has a fun, short ride. / Once he is done, Sam pets the horse and says, "Thank you." / Sam has a whole, fine time at the farm.

read:L3.09:B:0.text: Kate has a list, so she goes to the store. / She gets corn, milk, and a snack from a stand. / Before she is done, she checks her list. / "I got what I came for," said Kate. / She goes to the front and gets a short line. / She is glad she made a trip to the store, because she got what she came for.

read:L3.10:A:0.text: It is play day at the park. / When rain starts, the class does not stay in — they play in the rain, and get wet from top to tail! / A snail comes on the wet path. / "There is a snail!" said Sam. / They wait for the rain to stop, then drink cold water and play again.

read:L3.10:B:0.text: Every day, Kate takes the train to her job. / Today, because rain made the stop wet, the train came late. / She had to wait, so she got a cup of hot water and a snack from a stand. / "I will just wait," she said to a man in line. / The train came, and Kate got a spot by chance.

read:L3.11:A:0.text: Sam and his team go to the beach. / When they see a green kite, they find a sweet, clean spot to sit. / "Let's eat lunch by the sea," said Sam. / They read a page and laugh at a funny bit. / A queen bee comes to see the sweet leaf, then goes home. / Sam and his team feel very happy after a fine day.

read:L3.11:B:0.text: Each week, Kate and her team clean the street by the shop. / When they meet at nine, each one has a task. / Kate likes to see the street stay neat when they are done. / "We laugh a lot, but we get the job done," said Kate. / At the end, the team sits and has a sweet snack, glad for a job well done.

read:L3.12:A:0.text: Sam and his dad walk to the pond with a fine boat. / When snow starts, the pond starts to glow white. / Because it is chilly, Sam puts on his coat and gets a snack of toast. / "Let's float the boat and see if it can go," said Dad. / The boat does float, and Sam claps and laughs. / They walk home, glad they came to play.

read:L3.12:B:0.text: Kate had to walk home since the road was slow with traffic. / She put on her coat, since it was chilly, and got a snack of toast at a stand. / Another man said, "This road is always slow at this time." / Kate did not mind — she got to see the snow glow as she walked. / By the time she got home, she felt glad.

read:L3.13:A:0.text: At night, Sam and his mom talk and gaze up at the sky. / Because the sky is bright, it glows white and high. / "Let's stay up a bit," said Mom. / They eat a slice of pie and talk of the sky. / Sam feels glad for this quiet, bright night with his mom.

read:L3.13:B:0.text: After a long shift, Kate and her friend Jane talk it over at night. / When they sit and gaze up, the sky is bright. / "I might take the job at another site," said Kate. / Jane said, "That is a big thing — talk to your team, then decide." / They eat a slice of pie and talk until it gets late.

read:L3.14:A:0.text: Sam and his mom go to buy a new bike. / "I want the blue one," said Sam. / The shop has a big, blue bike that is true to what Sam likes. / Sam's mom said, "Let's buy it, then get a snack." / They get a bag of fruit and chew on it as they walk home with the new bike.

read:L3.14:B:0.text: Because she had a big meeting, Kate had to buy a new suit. / She went to a shop and got a blue suit that fit true to size. / "This one is right for you," said the person at the shop. / Kate said, "That is true, I will buy this one." / She got a snack of fruit on her way home, glad to have a new suit for the big day.

read:L3.15:A:0.text: At night, Sam and his dad look up at the moon. / "It is a good, cool night to look at the moon," said Dad. / They sit and look for as long as they can, because the moon is so bright. / Sam has a thing to think of: "What is the moon made of?" / Dad said, "That is a good thing to think of — let's find the answer in a book." / They read a book and find the answer, glad they took the time to look.

read:L3.15:B:0.text: After her shift, Kate likes to sit in her room and read a good book. / When it is cool at night, she gets a hot cup and takes a look at her book. / She took a class once on this same topic, but a book gives her time to think it over. / "I find the answer to a lot of things in a good book," she said. / Soon, she is deep in the pages, glad for a quiet night.

read:L3.16:A:0.text: It is a wild, cold day, and Sam and his mom go for a walk. / They see a child with a gold kite, and the wind is strong. / "Hold my hand," said Mom, "because the wind is wild today." / Sam is glad she told him to hold on. / They walk the whole way home, and Sam feels most glad once they are back and warm.

read:L3.16:B:0.text: Kate lost her old job when the shop closed, so she must find a new one. / Because she is bold, she does not quit — she sends her whole plan to ten shops. / One shop gets back to her and gives her a spot to start. / "I am so glad I did not lose hope," said Kate, most glad to have a new start. / Kate holds on to the good news the whole day.

read:L3.17:A:0.text: Once, Sam and his family took a whole day just for fun. / At home, Sam ate a bowl of oats and a slice of toast. / Then they went to see a tiger and a robot at a big show. / Sam's eye spotted a huge, gold kite flying high in the sky. / "How very great!" said Sam, and his mom gave him a hug. / Next, they got a snack — a bag of fruit and a sweet, cold treat. / While busy people were there too, Sam felt happy and free. / They went home and read a good book close by the tree. / "This was the best day," said Sam. / His mom said, "I am very glad, too." / They ate a bite of pie, and Sam fell asleep, smiling, once his whole busy, great day was done.

read:L3.17:B:0.text: Once, Kate had a whole day off, and she made the most of it. / She woke up, made a cup of tea, and ate a slice of toast. / At nine, she met her team to help clean up the street — a job she likes since it feels like a great use of a free day. / By noon, the whole team had made the place look neat, and people walking by said, "How nice!" / Kate felt very glad and a bit sleepy, but in a good way. / She got a snack of fruit and a cold drink, then sat and read a good book. / "Today was busy, but it was a great day," said Kate. / Once the sun set, she felt so glad she had spent her whole day well.

read:L4.01:A:0.text: Sam and his dad live on a farm.

read:L4.01:A:1.text: At dark, they walk to the yard.

read:L4.01:A:10.text: The farm is still, and the stars spark and shine in the dark yard.

read:L4.01:A:2.text: Sam can see a big, bright star.

read:L4.01:A:3.text: "That star is so very far," Dad said.

read:L4.01:A:4.text: Sam runs to get his cart.

read:L4.01:A:5.text: He puts a jar, a hard hat, and a sharp pencil in the cart.

read:L4.01:A:6.text: He wants to make a star chart.

read:L4.01:A:7.text: Dad helps Sam mark each star on the chart.

read:L4.01:A:8.text: "You are a smart artist," Dad said.

read:L4.01:B:1.text: Khan drives his car to the market.

read:L4.01:B:10.text: Khan is glad he did not start so late.

read:L4.01:B:2.text: He must park in the car park at the back.

read:L4.01:B:3.text: It is hard to find a spot — the car park is full.

read:L4.01:B:5.text: Khan spots a gap by the yard.

read:L4.01:B:6.text: He parks his car, locks it, and walks to the market.

read:L4.01:B:7.text: He needs a jar of jam, a sharp pencil, and a tiny chart for his garden.

read:L4.01:B:8.text: On the way back, a spark of light catches his eye — the sun is starting to sink behind the dark market roofs.

read:L4.02:A:0.text: It is harvest time on the farm.

read:L4.02:A:1.text: Dad and Sam load the cart before the storm starts.

read:L4.02:A:10.text: "More corn for us to sort tomorrow."

read:L4.02:A:2.text: Sam picks corn from the yard.

read:L4.02:A:3.text: His dog Storm (yes, that is her name!) runs to the barn.

read:L4.02:A:4.text: "A storm is coming, Storm!" Sam yells.

read:L4.02:A:5.text: The wind is strong, and rain starts to come down fast.

read:L4.02:A:6.text: Dad and Sam sort the corn and put it in the fort — a tiny shed by the barn.

read:L4.02:A:7.text: Storm the dog barks at the wind.

read:L4.02:A:8.text: Soon the storm is gone, and the sun shows itself again from the north.

read:L4.02:A:9.text: "That was a short storm," Sam says.

read:L4.02:B:1.text: Before she starts the car, she checks the horn and the fuel.

read:L4.02:B:2.text: The road has a fork — one way goes north, one goes to the port.

read:L4.02:B:4.text: A storm starts, and rain comes down hard and hits the window.

read:L4.02:B:5.text: Amina slows the car and clicks on the lights.

read:L4.02:B:6.text: At last, she spots the store where she must stop for parts for the fort's old gate.

read:L4.02:B:7.text: She picks four parts, pays, and starts the drive back.

read:L4.02:B:8.text: "That was a short but hard trip," she tells her boss.

read:L4.02:B:9.text: "I will need more time for the next one."

read:L4.03:A:1.text: Nadia's dad set up a bird perch by the porch.

read:L4.03:A:10.text: Nadia and her sister sat under the tree until the sun went down.

read:L4.03:A:2.text: Nadia sat still, waiting for her first bird to land.

read:L4.03:A:3.text: First a big black bird sat on the fence.

read:L4.03:A:4.text: Then a tiny bird with a red chest came to perch.

read:L4.03:A:6.text: Its chirp is so soft," Nadia said.

read:L4.03:A:7.text: Her sister ran to see too.

read:L4.03:A:8.text: "Don't stir, or it will fly off," Nadia told her.

read:L4.03:A:9.text: The bird did not fly off — it stayed and had a drink, then flew off with a quick turn.

read:L4.03:B:2.text: First, he checks each person's chart.

read:L4.03:B:3.text: Then he helps a girl with a hurt arm — she fell by the curb and needs a splint.

read:L4.03:B:4.text: "Try not to stir it too much," Bilal tells her.

read:L4.03:B:5.text: Her mother sits with her, holding her purse.

read:L4.03:B:6.text: Later, an older man comes in with a bad thirst and a fever.

read:L4.03:B:7.text: Bilal checks his term of illness and rings the doctor.

read:L4.03:B:8.text: By the end of his shift, Bilal is tired, but glad he could help.

read:L4.03:B:9.text: "Nursing is hard work," he tells his sister that night, "but I would not turn back."

read:L4.04:A:0.text: On a cold, clear day, Hina and her dad hike near the hills.

read:L4.04:A:1.text: Hina wears a warm coat and a hat, but no gloves — she likes to feel the crisp air.

read:L4.04:A:2.text: "Look — a deer!" Dad says, showing her.

read:L4.04:A:3.text: It is a rare deer with pale hair on its back.

read:L4.04:A:5.text: It stares at Hina, its ears turning this way and that.

read:L4.04:A:6.text: Hina stands still and does not dare move.

read:L4.04:A:7.text: After a year of hiking with her dad, this is the closest she has come to a deer.

read:L4.04:A:8.text: "I will never forget this," Hina says.

read:L4.04:A:9.text: On the walk back, they share a pear and talk of the deer the whole way home.

read:L4.04:B:0.text: Farah works at a tiny shop that sells chairs and tables.

read:L4.04:B:1.text: It is a warm day, and the work is hard.

read:L4.04:B:2.text: A pair of chairs must be moved to the back room, and Farah has to clear a path first.

read:L4.04:B:3.text: "Be careful — that chair leg is not square," her boss warns.

read:L4.04:B:4.text: Farah takes care, but her arms still hurt by the end of her shift.

read:L4.04:B:5.text: By closing time, a man comes in to buy a rare, old chair worth a fair price.

read:L4.04:B:6.text: Farah helps him carry it to his car.

read:L4.04:B:7.text: "That was the worst part of my day, but also the best sale," she tells her sister that night, and they share a laugh.

read:L4.05:A:0.text: Zayn is a boy who makes a lot of noise.

read:L4.05:A:1.text: In class, his choice seat is next to the window, and he likes to spot every bird, truck, and train he sees.

read:L4.05:A:2.text: "Zayn, use a soft voice," his teacher says.

read:L4.05:A:3.text: At recess, Zayn and his friends toss a coin to pick a game.

read:L4.05:A:5.text: Tails, we play with the toy trucks," Zayn says.

read:L4.05:A:7.text: Zayn grins big and runs to get the toy box.

read:L4.05:A:8.text: His friend Roy joins in, and soon the whole class is enjoying the game.

read:L4.05:A:9.text: By the end of recess, Zayn's voice is quite tired from cheering.

read:L4.05:B:0.text: Tariq works at a shop that fixes engines.

read:L4.05:B:1.text: Today, he must make a choice: fix an old engine's oil leak, or help a customer who needs a new coin battery for her car key.

read:L4.05:B:3.text: Roy, tells him to help the customer first.

read:L4.05:B:4.text: Tariq checks the car key, finds the right coin battery, and fits it in.

read:L4.05:B:5.text: "That should not annoy you again," he tells her.

read:L4.05:B:6.text: Then Tariq turns to the oil leak — it takes him a good while to find the moist patch under the engine and seal the joint.

read:L4.05:B:7.text: By the end of the day, Tariq feels the joy of a job done well, even when his voice is tired from talking to so many customers.

read:L4.06:A:0.text: It was a bright, loud day at the county fair.

read:L4.06:A:1.text: Bilal and his mom walked past a brown cow, a tiny mouse in a cage, and a fluffy owl blinking in the sun.

read:L4.06:A:2.text: Then a clown in a big gown and a bright crown came by, honking a horn.

read:L4.06:A:3.text: "That is so loud!" Bilal said, covering his mouth.

read:L4.06:A:4.text: The clown made a crowd of kids laugh out loud.

read:L4.06:A:5.text: A dog started to howl at the clown's honking horn, and an owl in a nearby cage let out a soft growl-like hoot.

read:L4.06:A:6.text: Bilal counted five clowns before he and his mom found their way to the food stand for a snack.

read:L4.06:B:0.text: It is a hot day, and Naveed is at work downtown when the power goes out.

read:L4.06:B:1.text: The whole office is dark, and a loud, low sound comes from the backup generator switching on.

read:L4.06:B:2.text: "How long will this last?" a coworker asks.

read:L4.06:B:3.text: Naveed checks his device — no signal, either.

read:L4.06:B:4.text: He walks down to the ground floor, where a tiny crowd has formed near the front doors.

read:L4.06:B:5.text: Someone found a radio and is counting down the minutes until the power comes back.

read:L4.06:B:6.text: After about an hour, the lights come back on, and a round of quiet cheers moves across the crowd.

read:L4.06:B:7.text: "I am proud we stayed so calm," Naveed's boss says as everyone heads back to their desks.

read:L4.07:A:0.text: At dawn, Zara and her granddad walk to the small lawn behind their house.

read:L4.07:A:1.text: A hawk lands on the old wall, its claw gripping the stone.

read:L4.07:A:2.text: "Don't move, or you'll cause it to fly off," her granddad whispers.

read:L4.07:A:4.text: The hawk turns its head, gives a small yawn, and looks right at her.

read:L4.07:A:5.text: Then it spreads its wings and flies over the mall down the road.

read:L4.07:A:6.text: "That was worth the early start!" Zara says.

read:L4.07:A:7.text: On the walk back, they talk about hawks and how they hunt.

read:L4.07:A:8.text: Zara makes a quick drawing of the hawk in her notebook before her meal.

read:L4.07:B:0.text: Mariam works at a small shop inside the mall.

read:L4.07:B:1.text: Business is slow, so she and her coworker take a pause to talk.

read:L4.07:B:2.text: "I saw a hawk on my walk to work this morning," Mariam says.

read:L4.07:B:3.text: "That's rare for downtown," her coworker replies.

read:L4.07:B:4.text: At noon, a small fault in the mall's power system causes all the lights to flicker, and a loud alarm sounds.

read:L4.07:B:5.text: "Don't fall over anyone — stay calm and walk to the hall," a staff member calls out.

read:L4.07:B:6.text: After a short pause, the power comes back, and the alarm stops.

read:L4.07:B:7.text: "Well, that was not part of the plan," Mariam laughs, and they get back to work.

read:L4.08:A:0.text: "Get ready — the weather is turning," Dad said, looking at the heavy gray clouds.

read:L4.08:A:1.text: Sana ran to get her coat.

read:L4.08:A:2.text: She had a small cut on her knee from playing outside, so Dad helped clean it first.

read:L4.08:A:3.text: "Don't rub it with dirty hands," he said, wrapping a bandage around her knee.

read:L4.08:A:4.text: Sana took a deep breath and looked out the window.

read:L4.08:A:5.text: Wind began to shake the thread-thin branches of the old tree.

read:L4.08:A:6.text: "I meant to bring in the washing before this," Mom said, dashing outside.

read:L4.08:A:7.text: By the time she got back, her hair was a mess, but the washing was safe and dry.

read:L4.08:A:8.text: That night, the family sat close, listening to the storm, glad to be warm and healthy inside.

read:L4.08:B:0.text: Rashid was driving to a job site when he took a wrong turn onto a bumpy road.

read:L4.08:B:1.text: His truck hit a deep rut, and his wrist twisted hard against the wheel.

read:L4.08:B:2.text: "That's not good," he said, feeling a sharp pain.

read:L4.08:B:3.text: He pulled over, took a breath, and checked his wrist — it was already starting to swell.

read:L4.08:B:4.text: Rashid called his boss to explain he would be late.

read:L4.08:B:5.text: At the clinic, a nurse wrapped his wrist and told him to rest it.

read:L4.08:B:6.text: "You're lucky it's not broken," she said.

read:L4.08:B:7.text: Rashid signed the form, thanked her, and called his boss again with an update.

rule:L2.06.text: Blends. Two consonants side by side keep BOTH sounds. Say them quickly, one after the other. FLOSS: after a short vowel at the end of a short word, f, l, s and z are doubled: stuff, smell, glass, buzz.

rule:L2.07.text: Final blends. At the end of a word two consonants keep both sounds: nest, hand, jump. FLOSS still holds: a short vowel then f, l, s or z at the end doubles it.

rule:L2.08.text: Three-letter blends. s plus a blend: three sounds said quickly, s-t-r in strap. shr and thr start with one digraph sound.

rule:L2.09.text: Adding -s and -es. Add -s to most words: cat, cats. Add -es after s, x, z, sh, ch and tch: it adds a syllable you can hear, wish, wishes.

rule:L2.10.text: Adding -ed. -ed says /t/ after p k f s sh ch (jumped), /d/ after voiced sounds (grinned), and /ed/ after t or d (wanted).

rule:L2.11.text: Adding -ing and -er. Read the base word, then add the ending. The base word does not change: jump, jumping, jumper.

rule:L2.12.text: Two-syllable words. Find the two vowels. Split between the two consonants in the middle: rab·bit, nap·kin. Read each part, then the whole word.

rule:L3.01.text: Silent e. The e at the end is silent. It jumps over one consonant and makes the vowel say its name: cap, cape.

rule:L3.02.text: Silent e. i_e: the e is silent and the i says its name: kit, kite.

rule:L3.03.text: Silent e. o_e, u_e and e_e work the same way: hop, hope; cub, cube.

rule:L3.04.text: Drop the e. Before an ending that starts with a vowel (-ing, -ed, -er), drop the silent e: hope, hoping.

rule:L3.05.text: Open syllables. A syllable that ends with a vowel is open: the vowel says its name. Try the first vowel open: ro·bot, mu·sic.

rule:L3.06.text: Y as a vowel. At the end of a short word y says /ī/: my. At the end of a longer word it says /ē/: happy.

rule:L3.07.text: Soft c and soft g. Before e, i or y, c says /s/ and g usually says /j/: city, cage. After a short vowel, /j/ is spelled -dge: bridge.

rule:L3.15.text: oo has two sounds. Try the long sound first, moon. If it is not a real word, flex to the short sound, book.

rule:L3.16.text: Long vowel families. In -ild, -ind, -old and -ost the vowel says its name even with no silent e: wild, kind, cold, most.

rule:L4.02.text: war and wor. After w, ar often sounds like or (warm) and or often sounds like er (work).

rule:L4.08.text: Silent letters. Some letter pairs keep only one sound: kn and gn say /n/, wr says /r/, mb says /m/.

rule:L4.09.text: ph, ch and gh. ph says /f/. ch can say /k/ (school) or /sh/ (chef). gh says /g/ at the start (ghost).

rule:L4.10.text: Consonant-le. A word ending in a consonant + le: that last chunk is one syllable, can·dle, ta·ble.

rule:L4.11.text: -tion, -sion, -ture. -tion and -sion say /shun/, -ture says /cher/, -ous says /us/. Read the ending as one chunk.

rule:L4.12.text: Breaking words apart. Mark the vowels. VC/CV: split between consonants (rab·bit). V/CV: try open first (ti·ger). If that is not a word, flex: cab·in. Unstressed vowels often say 'uh'.

rule:L4.13.text: Suffix spelling. 1-1-1: one syllable, one vowel, one final consonant: double it (run, running). Consonant + y: change y to i (happy, happier). Silent e: drop it (hope, hoping).

rule:L4.14.text: The word-attack routine. 1 Mark the vowels. 2 Peel off prefixes and suffixes. 3 Chunk the middle into syllables. 4 Blend the chunks. 5 Flex if it is not a real word.

rule:L4.15.text: Unknown words. Do not guess from the picture or the first letter. Use the routine: vowels, peel, chunk, blend, flex. Then check: does it make sense here?

ss:L5.01:prime:q.text: Have you ever seen rain, or watched a cloud form? What did it look like?

ss:L5.01:text:0:0.text: Every morning the sun comes up and warms the sea. The warm water turns into something you cannot see — water vapor. It floats up into the sky, where the air is cooler. Up there the vapor gathers into tiny drops, and the tiny drops make a cloud. A cloud is just millions of tiny drops of water, all floating together.

ss:L5.01:text:0:1.text: The cloud gets heavier and heavier as more drops join it. Soon the drops are too heavy to float. They fall — as rain, or snow if the air is very cold. The rain falls on the hills and the fields and the roofs of houses. Some of it soaks into the ground. Some of it runs into rivers. The rivers carry it back to the sea. And then, gradually, the sun warms the sea again, and the whole thing starts over. This is called the water cycle, because it never really stops — it just goes around and around, again and again, forever.

ss:L5.01:text:0:q0.text: What does the sun do to the sea water?

ss:L5.01:text:0:q1.text: What falls out of a heavy cloud?

ss:L5.01:text:0:q2.text: Why do you think the passage calls it a "cycle" instead of just "the weather"?

ss:L5.01:text:1:0.text: A farmer checks the sky every morning, because the sky can tell her a lot.

ss:L5.01:text:1:1.text: Each day, the sun heats the ocean and the wet fields, and some of that water turns into vapor. Vapor is water you cannot see, and it rises into the air.

ss:L5.01:text:1:2.text: You cannot see vapor, but you can see what it makes. High in the sky, the air is cooler, so the vapor cools down too. It turns back into tiny drops of water, and billions of these tiny drops make one cloud.

ss:L5.01:text:1:3.text: A cloud can only hold so much water. When it holds too much, the drops fall as rain.

ss:L5.01:text:1:4.text: For a farmer, rain at the right time can mean a good harvest. Rain at the wrong time, or no rain at all, can ruin a whole crop.

ss:L5.01:text:1:5.text: This is why many farms build reservoirs. A reservoir is a large lake that stores rainwater during the wet season. During the dry season, farmers use that stored water to water their fields, instead of waiting for rain to fall at exactly the right moment.

ss:L5.01:text:1:6.text: Any rain that is not stored soaks into the soil, or runs into a river. Rivers carry that water back to the sea, and then the sun warms the sea again, and the whole cycle starts over.

ss:L5.01:text:1:7.text: For anyone who depends on rain to earn a living, understanding this cycle is not just science. It is practical knowledge, passed down for many years.

ss:L5.02:text:0:0.text: A long time ago, people did not have money like we do now. Say a farmer had extra eggs. He needed shoes. He had to find a shoemaker who wanted eggs that day. This was called bartering. It means trading one thing for another thing. It worked, but it was slow. It was often inconvenient. What if the shoemaker did not want eggs that week?

ss:L5.02:text:0:1.text: So people started using something everyone agreed was valuable. At first, they used things like shells, salt, or metal rings. Later, countries began making coins. They began printing paper money too. Each note had a promise on it. It said, this piece of paper is worth this much.

ss:L5.02:text:0:2.text: Now the farmer could sell his eggs for money. He could use that money to buy shoes from anyone. He could buy them anywhere. He could buy them any time. Money did not replace bartering because bartering was wrong. It replaced bartering because money is more convenient.

ss:L5.02:text:0:3.text: Today, many people do not even carry coins. They use cards or phones to send money fast. But it is still the same idea. People figured this out thousands of years ago.

ss:L5.02:text:0:q1.text: Why did people start using coins instead of bartering?

ss:L5.02:text:0:q2.text: The text says money "is still the same idea" as thousands of years ago — what idea is that?

ss:L5.02:text:1:0.text: Every payday, a worker trades hours of work for money. This feels normal today. But it is newer than most people think, and it solved a real problem.

ss:L5.02:text:1:1.text: Before money existed, people bartered. Bartering means trading one thing directly for another. A carpenter might trade a chair for a sack of flour. But this only worked if the baker needed a chair that same week. Most of the time, the two people did not want the same things at the same time. So trade was slow. Often, it did not happen at all.

ss:L5.02:text:1:2.text: Money solved this problem. A worker could sell their labor for money. Then they could use that money to buy whatever they needed, whenever they needed it. The other person did not need to want the worker's exact skill in return. They just had to accept money, because everyone else accepted it too.

ss:L5.02:text:1:3.text: Today, much of this happens without cash at all. Wages arrive in a bank account or a mobile wallet. Payments move with a single tap. But the idea underneath is exactly the same. Money is a trusted token that everyone agrees to accept. That is the same idea that solved the carpenter's problem, long before banks existed.

ss:L5.02:text:1:4.text: Understanding this idea makes it easier to understand other money topics too, like saving, borrowing, and interest. All of them depend on one thing: how well that trusted token holds its value over time.

ss:L5.03:prime:1.text: it never stops your whole life

ss:L5.03:prime:2.text: doctors and nurses check it constantly using nothing but two fingers and a watch.

ss:L5.03:prime:q.text: Have you ever felt your own pulse before? Where did you check it?

ss:L5.03:text:0:0.text: Put your hand on your chest. Can you feel it? Thump, thump, thump. That is your heart. It never stops working. Not even for one second, your whole life. Your heart is about the size of your closed fist. Its job is to be a pump. It pushes blood all around your body. It uses long, thin tubes called blood vessels.

ss:L5.03:text:0:1.text: Inside your heart there are four rooms. We call them chambers. Blood comes in from your body. It is low on oxygen. The heart sends it to your lungs. There it picks up fresh oxygen. Then the blood comes back to the heart. The heart pushes it out again. It goes to every part of you. It goes to your brain, your fingers, and your toes. It carries fresh oxygen to keep every part of you working. Blood goes around this whole loop about once every minute. That is why oxygen is so vital. Without it, your body's parts cannot do their jobs. A doctor listening to your heartbeat is really listening to that pump. It works over and over, to keep you alive.

ss:L5.03:text:0:q0.text: How many chambers does the heart have?

ss:L5.03:text:0:q1.text: Why does blood go to the lungs before going to the rest of the body?

ss:L5.03:text:0:q2.text: Why does the text say oxygen is "vital"?

ss:L5.03:text:1:0.text: Anyone can check how hard their heart is working. You only need two fingers and a watch.

ss:L5.03:text:1:1.text: Press your first two fingers gently on the inside of your wrist, just below your thumb. Or press them against the side of your neck. You will feel a steady beat. This is your pulse. Each beat is one push of your heart, sending blood out into your body.

ss:L5.03:text:1:2.text: A resting adult heart usually beats sixty to a hundred times a minute. A lower number, within reason, is often a sign of a fit heart. Regular exercise trains the heart muscle. A trained heart can pump more blood with each beat. So it does not need to beat as often to circulate the same amount of blood.

ss:L5.03:text:1:3.text: A higher number can mean stress, illness, too much caffeine, or simply climbing a flight of stairs. The number alone does not tell the whole story.

ss:L5.03:text:1:4.text: Doctors and nurses check pulse all the time. It is one of the fastest, cheapest ways to learn something important about a person's health, without any equipment beyond a watch.

ss:L5.03:text:1:5.text: Knowing your own normal resting pulse is useful. Check it while you are resting, not right after activity. This gives you a baseline. If your pulse ever feels clearly different from normal, especially if it feels uneven rather than just fast or slow, it is worth mentioning to a doctor. Do not just ignore it.

ss:L5.03:text:1:q0.text: Where can you check your pulse?

ss:L5.03:text:1:q1.text: Why might a trained heart beat slower at rest?

ss:L5.03:text:1:q2.text: What does the text say is worth mentioning to a doctor?

ss:L5.03:vocab:1.text: circulate. to move around continuously, through a system, and come back to where it started.. Blood circulates through your body, carrying oxygen to every part. Rumors can circulate around a school in a single day.

ss:L5.04:text:0:0.text: NARRATOR: Zara was digging in the garden when her spade hit something hard.

ss:L5.04:text:0:1.text: ZARA: Uncle Tariq! Come look. There's something buried here!

ss:L5.04:text:0:10.text: TARIQ: Exactly. Every piece like this is evidence. Archaeologists dig very carefully. They do not want to misplace or damage anything. Each piece helps us understand people who lived here long ago.

ss:L5.04:text:0:11.text: ZARA: I'm not going to overlook anything else in this garden ever again!

ss:L5.04:text:0:12.text: NARRATOR: And from that day, Zara looked at the ground a little differently. She wondered what other ancient stories might be buried just beneath her feet.

ss:L5.04:text:0:2.text: TARIQ: (kneeling down) Let's see. This looks like a piece of old pottery. Look at that pattern on it.

ss:L5.04:text:0:3.text: ZARA: Is it valuable? Like treasure?

ss:L5.04:text:0:4.text: TARIQ: Maybe more valuable than treasure. This could be evidence. It could show us something ancient. People lived here thousands of years ago.

ss:L5.04:text:0:5.text: NARRATOR: Uncle Tariq turned the piece over carefully in his hands.

ss:L5.04:text:0:6.text: TARIQ: A long time ago, people lived right here. We call them the Indus Valley Civilization. It is one of the oldest in the world. It is as old as ancient Egypt.

ss:L5.04:text:0:7.text: ZARA: Did they have houses? Did they have cities?

ss:L5.04:text:0:8.text: TARIQ: They had huge, carefully planned cities. They had straight streets. They had brick houses. They even had a way to carry dirty water away, under the ground. That kept the streets clean. That is evidence that they were very organized.

ss:L5.04:text:0:9.text: ZARA: (overjoyed) So this old broken piece of pottery is a clue?

ss:L5.04:text:1:0.text: NARRATOR: A radio interview, recorded on-site at an archaeological dig.

ss:L5.04:text:1:1.text: HOST: I'm standing at an important dig site. Dr. Ahmed, for listeners who have never heard of the Indus Valley Civilization, what are we looking at?

ss:L5.04:text:1:2.text: AHMED: We're looking at the remains of one of the world's oldest cities. It's about four and a half thousand years old. That's roughly the same age as ancient Egypt. What's most striking isn't just its age. It's how organized it was.

ss:L5.04:text:1:3.text: HOST: Organized how? When I think "ancient civilization," I picture something a bit more... rough and simple.

ss:L5.04:text:1:4.text: AHMED: That's a common misunderstanding. The evidence proves it wrong. These cities had straight streets, laid out in a grid. They used bricks of the same size across huge distances. They even had covered drains running under the streets, to carry dirty water away. Some cities elsewhere would not have anything like that again for thousands of years.

ss:L5.04:text:1:5.text: HOST: What convinced you this wasn't just a guess based on a few old ruins?

ss:L5.04:text:1:6.text: AHMED: Fair question. We don't want to overreach past what the evidence actually shows. But we're talking about two major cities, far apart, with almost the same city plan. That is not an accident. It points to shared standards and shared knowledge.

ss:L5.04:text:1:7.text: HOST: And yet we still don't fully know what happened to them.

ss:L5.04:text:1:8.text: AHMED: Correct. That mystery is real, and I won't pretend we know more than we do. What we do know, we know from evidence: pottery, seals, city layouts, tools. What we don't yet know, we're honest about not knowing. That's what keeps people like me digging.

ss:L5.05:prime:q.text: Has the weather ever surprised you by being very different from what's typical for the season?

ss:L5.05:text:0:0.text: "Weather" and "climate" sound almost the same. But they answer two different questions. Weather is what's happening outside right now, or this week. Is it raining? Is it sunny? Is it cold or warm? Weather can change very fast. It can be sunny in the morning. It can be rainy by afternoon. It can be different again tomorrow. That's why weather forecasters can only predict a few days ahead. It's a fast-changing system. It's hard to predict far into the future.

ss:L5.05:text:0:1.text: Climate is different. Climate is the usual pattern of weather in a place. We measure it over many, many years. A desert's climate is usually hot and dry. That doesn't mean it never rains there. It means rain is rare, on average, over time. A place near the ocean usually has a mild climate. It is not too hot, and not too cold. This is true even though its daily weather still changes from day to day.

ss:L5.05:text:0:2.text: So if someone asks, "what's the weather like?" they want to know about today. If they ask, "what's the climate like?" they want to know about the usual pattern, over many years, not just today.

ss:L5.05:text:0:q2.text: Why can forecasters only reliably predict a few days ahead?

ss:L5.05:text:1:0.text: News reports sometimes mix up two words. The words are weather and climate. They do not mean the same thing.

ss:L5.05:text:1:1.text: Weather means what is happening in one place right now. It means the temperature, the rain, and the wind, on a given day. Weather is hard to predict far ahead. Small changes today can lead to very different results a week later. Even the best forecasts get shaky after about ten days.

ss:L5.05:text:1:2.text: Climate is different. Climate is the usual pattern of weather in a region. It is measured over many years, not one day. A region's climate does not tell you tomorrow's weather. It tells you the chances of different kinds of weather over a long time.

ss:L5.05:text:1:3.text: This difference matters in real life. Say it snows during a week that is usually warm. That is just one weather event. It does not prove the climate is changing. One cold day does not undo the fact that summer, on average, is hotter than winter.

ss:L5.05:text:1:4.text: Knowing this difference is a useful skill. It lets you read a headline about one storm without panicking. A single event tells you about today. It does not tell you much about the bigger, longer pattern.

ss:L5.05:text:1:q2.text: What example does the text give of a weather event that doesn't prove the climate is changing?

ss:L5.06:prime:0.text: water can be solid (ice), liquid (water), or gas (vapor/steam)

ss:L5.06:prime:1.text: heat and cold are what change it from one to another.

ss:L5.06:prime:q.text: Have you ever seen a window fog up, or a cold drink 'sweat'? What do you think causes that?

ss:L5.06:text:0:0.text: Water can be three different things. It changes from one to another just by getting hotter or colder. As ice, water is a solid. It is hard and cold. It keeps its own shape. Melt the ice, and it transforms into liquid water. It is still the same water, just warmer. Now it flows. It takes the shape of whatever holds it. Heat that water even more, all the way to boiling. It transforms again, into steam. Steam is a gas. Steam is invisible water vapor. The little cloud you see above a boiling pot is not the vapor itself. It is tiny water droplets. They have already cooled and formed again in the cooler air.

ss:L5.06:text:0:1.text: This is exactly what happens in the water cycle you learned about earlier. The sun heats water until it transforms into invisible vapor. The vapor rises. Higher up, the air is colder. So the vapor transforms back into tiny liquid droplets. That is a cloud. It is the same water, but three different forms. It changes back and forth, depending only on how hot or cold it is.

ss:L5.06:text:0:q0.text: Name the three forms water can take.

ss:L5.06:text:0:q1.text: What makes water change from one form to another?

ss:L5.06:text:0:q2.text: The text says the cloud above a boiling pot isn't the vapor itself — what is it?

ss:L5.06:text:1:0.text: On a cold morning, the inside of a window can fog up. The outside stays clear. This is a small, everyday example of the same physics behind the whole water cycle.

ss:L5.06:text:1:1.text: The air inside a warm room holds invisible water vapor. It comes from cooking, from breathing, even from a kettle boiled earlier. Warm air can hold more water vapor than cold air can. When that warm, vapor-carrying air touches a cold surface, like a window with cold air outside, it cools down fast, right at that surface.

ss:L5.06:text:1:2.text: Cooled air cannot hold as much vapor. So the extra vapor turns back into liquid water. This is called condensation, and it happens right there on the glass. It is the same change that forms a cloud. It is just happening on your window instead of high in the sky.

ss:L5.06:text:1:3.text: This is also why a cold drink sweats on a hot day. It is why bathroom mirrors fog up after a shower. Builders even worry about condensation forming inside walls, where nobody can see it or wipe it away.

ss:L5.06:text:1:4.text: Understanding this is genuinely useful. A dehumidifier works by cooling air on purpose, to force this same condensation to happen. Then it drains the water away. This actually removes moisture from a room, instead of just hiding the problem.

ss:L5.07:text:0:0.text: Zeenat had five hundred rupees from her birthday. She wanted to decide what to do with it. Her mother had an idea. Instead of spending it all right away, she could put some of it in a savings account at the bank. It would stay safe there. It would even grow, a little, all on its own.

ss:L5.07:text:0:1.text: "How can money grow on its own?" Zeenat asked. It was a very sensible question. Her mother explained that banks pay you interest. This is a small extra amount for keeping your money with them. It gets added regularly. The bank uses your saved money to lend to other people. Then it shares a bit of what it earns back with you. It is not a huge amount, especially at first. But it adds up over time.

ss:L5.07:text:0:2.text: Zeenat decided on a simple plan. It was her own small budget. She would spend half of her birthday money on something fun, right away. She would save the other half. She would check on it every few months, to watch it grow, bit by bit. It was not a hard decision once she thought about it that way. Some now, some later, and a small reward just for being patient.

ss:L5.07:text:0:q0.text: What does the bank pay you for keeping your money there?

ss:L5.07:text:0:q1.text: What was Zeenat's simple budget plan?

ss:L5.07:text:0:q2.text: Why does the text say interest "isn't a huge amount, especially at first"?

ss:L5.07:text:1:0.text: Understanding interest is one of the most useful things an adult can know about money. It comes down to one key idea: simple interest versus compound interest.

ss:L5.07:text:1:1.text: Simple interest is easy. It is counted only on the amount you first saved or borrowed. Compound interest works differently. It is counted on that first amount, plus any interest you have already earned. In other words, your interest starts to earn its own interest.

ss:L5.07:text:1:2.text: That small difference matters a lot over time. Even a modest amount, saved often, can grow into a large sum if you give it compound interest and many years. This is why starting to save early matters more than the size of any one deposit.

ss:L5.07:text:1:3.text: The same idea works against you with debt. An unpaid credit card bill also grows through compound interest. If you only pay the minimum each month, that debt can grow fast, and it can catch people by surprise.

ss:L5.07:text:1:4.text: A simple budget helps with both sides of this. Here is one approach that works well. First, pay for the essentials: rent, food, and bills. Next, set aside a fixed amount for savings, right away. Only after that, decide what is left for everything else. Do not just save whatever happens to be left at the end of the month. For most people, that amount is close to nothing. A fixed plan, made once, removes the need to decide it again every month.

ss:L5.08:text:0:0.text: NARRATOR: Bilal was out of breath after just one lap around the field.

ss:L5.08:text:0:1.text: BILAL: (panting) Coach, is it bad that my heart is beating so fast?

ss:L5.08:text:0:10.text: SANA: A heartbeat is one of the best, simplest clues your body gives you about itself. Ready for one more lap — moderate pace this time?

ss:L5.08:text:0:2.text: SANA: Not at all — that's exactly what your heart is supposed to do when you run. It's working harder, pumping more blood, so your muscles get more oxygen. That fast heartbeat is your heart doing its job well.

ss:L5.08:text:0:3.text: BILAL: But it feels like it's about to interrupt itself or something!

ss:L5.08:text:0:4.text: SANA: (laughing) It won't. A healthy heart can speed up a lot during exercise and then calm back down afterward. That "calming back down" part matters too — it tells us something.

ss:L5.08:text:0:5.text: BILAL: What does it tell us?

ss:L5.08:text:0:6.text: SANA: The faster your heart rate comes back down to normal after exercise, the fitter your heart usually is. It's like your heart's own forecast for how strong it's getting.

ss:L5.08:text:0:7.text: BILAL: So I should run every day, as hard as I can, forever?

ss:L5.08:text:0:8.text: SANA: Not extreme — moderate. Regular movement, most days, is essential. But your body also needs rest to recover. Exercise, and rest, work together — you can't foresee good fitness from just one without the other.

ss:L5.08:text:1:0.text: NARRATOR: An annual check-up, at a small clinic.

ss:L5.08:text:1:1.text: FATIMA: Your blood pressure and resting heart rate both look good this year, Mr. Rizvi. Whatever you're doing, keep doing it.

ss:L5.08:text:1:2.text: RIZVI: Honestly, I started walking most mornings. About thirty minutes. Nothing extreme. I didn't want to interrupt my whole routine.

ss:L5.08:text:1:3.text: FATIMA: That's exactly the right kind of activity. Moderate, but done often. That makes the biggest difference for most people. More than any hard, short-term push. Doing it often matters more than doing it hard, for heart health.

ss:L5.08:text:1:4.text: RIZVI: Can you forecast anything from these numbers? Is there anything I should worry about?

ss:L5.08:text:1:5.text: FATIMA: I can't foretell the future from just one check-up. I wouldn't pretend to. But these numbers, tracked over time, tell us far more than any single visit. That's why we check every year, not just once.

ss:L5.08:text:1:6.text: RIZVI: Is there anything I should watch for between now and next year?

ss:L5.08:text:1:7.text: FATIMA: A few things. Chest discomfort that interrupts normal activity. Unusual shortness of breath. Or a heartbeat that feels uneven, not just fast. Any of those, don't wait for your next visit. Come in right away. Otherwise, keep the walks, keep it moderate, and I will see you in a year.

ss:L5.08:text:1:8.text: RIZVI: That's a relief. I half-expected a lecture.

ss:L5.08:text:1:9.text: FATIMA: The lecture is only for people who aren't already doing the essential thing. You are. Keep at it.

ss:L5.09:text:0:0.text: Imagine walking through Mohenjo-daro. It is a real, ancient city. It is almost 4,500 years old. The streets are straight. They cross each other like a grid, just like graph paper. Most houses are built from the same size of baked brick. This is true all across the city, not just in one part. This is widespread. It tells us people agreed on shared rules for building.

ss:L5.09:text:0:1.text: One building stood out the most. It was a large pool called the Great Bath. It was big enough for several people. It may have been used for special occasions, not just everyday washing. Nearby, huge brick buildings stored grain. Grain was a resource every city needed, in case of a bad harvest year.

ss:L5.09:text:0:2.text: But the most surprising clue is not a building at all. It is tiny stone seals. They are carved with pictures of animals and symbols. Nobody has fully read these symbols yet. The same style of seal has been found far away, in ancient Mesopotamia. That place is hundreds of kilometers away, across land and sea. This widespread trade tells us something important. Indus Valley traders were not alone. They were connected to a much bigger, ancient world.

ss:L5.09:text:0:q0.text: What tells us people across the whole city "agreed on shared rules for building"?

ss:L5.09:text:0:q1.text: What was the Great Bath possibly used for?

ss:L5.09:text:0:q2.text: What do the seals found far away, in Mesopotamia, suggest?

ss:L5.09:text:1:0.text: Stone weights sound like a boring kind of evidence. But they turn out to be one of the most important clues we have.

ss:L5.09:text:1:1.text: Across Indus Valley cities, hundreds of kilometers apart, archaeologists have found stone weights that follow the same pattern. This is a strong sign of a shared system. It was not just separate local habits in each city.

ss:L5.09:text:1:2.text: This matters for a simple reason. Trade only works well when both sides trust the measurement. A trader moving between cities needed to know one thing. A weight called by one name meant the same real amount everywhere. Without that trust, every trade would need to start from nothing, every time. The same idea applies to bricks. Cities across the whole civilization used bricks of the same standard sizes. That kind of planning only makes sense if there was some shared authority. Or at least a shared way of doing things, linking cities that were far apart.

ss:L5.09:text:1:3.text: The clearest evidence for trade with other lands is a set of small stone seals. Each seal is carved with an animal and a script nobody has fully read yet. Nearly the same style of seal has been found far away, in ancient Mesopotamia. This suggests a real trade network. It stretched across the sea and up through the Persian Gulf. It was working about four and a half thousand years ago.

ss:L5.09:text:1:q0.text: Why does the text say trust in measurement matters for trade?

ss:L5.09:text:1:q1.text: What does using the same brick sizes across far-apart cities suggest?

ss:L5.09:text:1:q2.text: Where has the same style of Indus seal been found, far from the Indus Valley?

ss:L5.10:prime:q.text: Have you ever changed a plan because of a weather forecast?

ss:L5.10:text:0:0.text: Every year, for a few months, the wind changes direction over South Asia. It brings something dramatic with it. We call it the monsoon. Here is how it works. During the hot months, the land heats up faster than the ocean does. Hot air over the land rises. To replace it, cooler, wet air rushes in from over the ocean. This air moves across the coast, straight onto land.

ss:L5.10:text:0:1.text: That ocean air carries an intense amount of moisture. It picked this up from months of sun heating the sea. As the air moves inland, it rises over hills and mountains. It cools down. All that moisture turns into thick, heavy clouds. These clouds bring sudden, intense rain. Sometimes it rains for days at a time.

ss:L5.10:text:0:2.text: The monsoon is not just dramatic weather. For farmers across the region, it is essential. Crops are planted to depend on this rain. It usually arrives on the same schedule every year. Too little rain, and crops can fail from drought. Too much rain, all at once, and rivers can overflow. Towns and fields can flood. Understanding the monsoon means understanding both its gift and its danger, at the same time.

ss:L5.10:text:0:q0.text: Why does cooler, moisture-heavy ocean air rush in during the monsoon?

ss:L5.10:text:0:q1.text: What happens to that moisture as the air rises over hills and mountains?

ss:L5.10:text:0:q2.text: Why does the text call the monsoon both "a gift and a danger"?

ss:L5.10:text:1:0.text: A storm does not appear at random. It forms because moisture, heat, and air pressure interact. This happens in a fairly predictable way. Warm, wet air rises when it meets cooler air. It also rises when hills push it upward. This is the same process behind the monsoon. It is just packed into a smaller, more intense system. As the warm air rises, it cools. Its moisture turns to water fast. This releases heat. The heat fuels the storm even more. It becomes a cycle that weather experts watch closely.

ss:L5.10:text:1:1.text: This is why storm forecasts give more than just "rain expected." They give wind direction. They give rainfall totals. They give the storm's speed. All of this affects real risk. A slow storm can drop far more total rain on one spot than a fast storm of the same strength. It simply spends more time over the same ground. This is a major cause of flooding. A simple rain number does not show this on its own.

ss:L5.10:text:1:2.text: For people living where monsoons happen, this detail is not just science talk. It helps a farmer decide when to plant. It helps a family decide to move valuables upstairs. It helps a local government decide to open flood shelters early. Reading a forecast closely, not just the headline, is a genuinely useful adult skill.

ss:L5.10:text:1:q0.text: What releases heat that "fuels the storm even more"?

ss:L5.10:text:1:q1.text: Why can a slow-moving storm cause more total rainfall than a fast-moving one of similar strength?

ss:L5.10:text:1:q2.text: What three examples does the text give of decisions this detail helps someone make?

ss:L5.11:prime:q.text: Have you ever looked up at night and wondered how far away a star or planet really is?

ss:L5.11:text:0:0.text: The sun is the center of our solar system. It is an enormous ball of burning gas. It is so large that more than a million Earths could fit inside it. Eight planets travel around the sun. Each one moves on its own path. We call this path an orbit. Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars are the four closest planets. They are rocky planets. Then come Jupiter and Saturn. These two are enormous planets made mostly of gas. Jupiter alone is bigger than all the other planets put together. Furthest out are Uranus and Neptune. They are icy and distant. They are so far from the sun that they get only a faint bit of its light and warmth.

ss:L5.11:text:0:1.text: Earth is special among all eight planets. As far as we know, it is the only one with the exact right conditions for life. It is not too close to the sun, and not too distant. It has liquid water and air we can breathe. If you tried to walk from the sun to Neptune, it would take longer than a human lifetime. It would take many lifetimes. That is how enormous the distances really are. Pictures in books make the planets look close together, in a neat little row. But that is not really true.

ss:L5.11:text:0:q0.text: How many planets orbit the sun?

ss:L5.11:text:0:q2.text: What does the text say makes Earth "special among all eight"?

ss:L5.11:text:1:0.text: Pictures of the solar system are almost always misleading in one way. They show the planets close together. A picture drawn at the real scale would be mostly empty space.

ss:L5.11:text:1:1.text: Here is a way to feel the real scale. Imagine shrinking the sun down to the size of a large orange. At that size, Earth would be a tiny grain of sand, about ten meters away. Jupiter is an enormous planet. Over a thousand Earths could fit inside it. At our shrunk-down scale, Jupiter would be a marble, about fifty meters from the orange. Neptune is the most distant planet. It would be a small pea, almost three hundred meters away. That is the length of several city blocks.

ss:L5.11:text:1:2.text: This is not just a fun fact. It is the whole reason space travel is so hard. Spacecraft travel at enormous speeds. But the distances are so vast that a trip to Mars, one of Earth's closest neighbors, still takes many months each way. A trip to a distant planet like Neptune has taken over ten years.

ss:L5.11:text:1:3.text: Knowing this scale changes how you read a space news story. "Reached the outer solar system" does not mean a short trip that just took a bit longer. It means something on a totally different scale of distance than anything most people travel in daily life.

ss:L5.11:text:1:q0.text: In the orange-sized-sun model, roughly how far away is Earth?

ss:L5.11:text:1:q1.text: Why does the text say pictures of the solar system are "almost always misleading"?

ss:L5.11:text:1:q2.text: Why does a trip to Neptune take over ten years?

ss:L5.12:text:0:0.text: NARRATOR: Hania stood proudly next to her science fair project. It was a small circuit with a battery, some wires, and a tiny light bulb.

ss:L5.12:text:0:1.text: KHAN: Can you inspect this circuit for me? Can you tell me how it works?

ss:L5.12:text:0:2.text: HANIA: Sure! The battery is like the "push." It pushes electricity through the wire. The wire is a path, like a road. It carries the electricity all the way around, in a loop. That is why it is called a circuit. "Circ" means circle. A circuit is a loop that goes around.

ss:L5.12:text:0:3.text: KHAN: And what happens when I break the loop, like this? (pretends to disconnect a wire)

ss:L5.12:text:0:4.text: HANIA: The light goes out! The electricity cannot move across a broken path. It needs the whole loop to work. It needs to be built as one complete shape.

ss:L5.12:text:0:5.text: KHAN: I respect that explanation. Very clear. What would happen with a superhero-strength battery instead of this small one?

ss:L5.12:text:0:6.text: HANIA: (laughing) It would probably burn out the little light bulb! Bigger isn't always better. This bulb is built to work with this exact amount of electricity. Not more.

ss:L5.12:text:0:7.text: KHAN: One more question. Why does the wire feel a little warm?

ss:L5.12:text:0:8.text: HANIA: Some electricity turns into heat as it moves through the wire. That is actually wasted energy. A more efficient circuit loses less heat. Real engineers try to fix that.

ss:L5.12:text:0:9.text: KHAN: Excellent. I'll happily construct a very good grade for this project.

ss:L5.12:text:1:0.text: NARRATOR: A routine home electrical inspection.

ss:L5.12:text:1:1.text: BAIG: Our electricity bill has gone up a lot this year. Can you inspect the wiring and tell me if something's wrong?

ss:L5.12:text:1:10.text: IMRAN: Not today. I'll still finish a full inspection, to be sure. But so far, this looks like an efficiency question, not a safety one.

ss:L5.12:text:1:2.text: IMRAN: I'll take a look. First question, though. Has anything new been installed? A new appliance, an air conditioner?

ss:L5.12:text:1:3.text: BAIG: We added a second air conditioner about six months ago, for the hot season.

ss:L5.12:text:1:4.text: IMRAN: That would explain a lot. Older AC units use a lot more electricity than newer ones do, to cool the same amount of air. The newer models are built differently inside, and it makes a real difference.

ss:L5.12:text:1:5.text: BAIG: So the wiring itself isn't the problem?

ss:L5.12:text:1:6.text: IMRAN: I still want to inspect it properly before I say that for sure. Faulty wiring is a real safety issue, not just a cost issue. But my first guess, based on what I'm seeing, is that the higher bill matches the new unit. Not a fault in your wiring.

ss:L5.12:text:1:7.text: BAIG: Is there anything I can do to make things more efficient, without buying a whole new unit?

ss:L5.12:text:1:8.text: IMRAN: A few things. Clean the filters often. Seal any gaps around doors and windows, so cool air doesn't leak out. And set it to a semi-cool setting, instead of the coldest setting all day. None of that needs any construction work. Just simple habits.

ss:L5.12:text:1:9.text: BAIG: That's a relief. I half-expected you to report some expensive structural problem.
