ss:L7.03:text:0:0.text: Source 3 — Richard Palmes, Boston merchant. From his sworn testimony at the soldiers' trial, as transcribed in the trial record (Boston, 1770). Quoted directly, in the original phrasing and spelling, from the primary-source transcription at bostonmassacre.net/trial/d-palmes.htm — see the precise source note below.

ss:L7.03:text:0:1.text: "I went to see what was the matter, and found Captain Preston at the head of six or eight soldiers... I asked him if the soldiers' guns were loaded. He answered they were. I asked him if they were going to fire upon the inhabitants. He answered by no means... I had not been there more than two minutes before I heard the word 'fire'... I heard the report of a gun... After that gun went off I heard the word fire, but who said it I know not... After that I turned and saw the Grenadier who fired first, attempting to prick me by the side of the Captain with his bayonet. I had a large stick in my hand. I struck over-hand and hit him on his left arm, and knocked his hand from his gun. Upon that I turned, thinking the other would do the same, and struck at anybody at first, and hit the Captain."

ss:L7.03:text:0:2.text: (Palmes also testified the whole encounter, from first shout to last shot, lasted "not more than three quarters of a minute in the whole.")

ss:L7.03:text:0:q0.text: Who is Palmes, when did he give this account (relative to the trial), and for what purpose was it recorded (sworn trial testimony, not a private diary)?

ss:L7.03:text:0:q1.text: In his own words, when did Palmes strike the soldier — before, or after, that soldier had already fired? What was Palmes' stated reason for striking him (read the sentence just before "I struck over-hand" again)?

ss:L7.03:text:0:q2.text: This is the teaching point: other, independent secondary accounts of this same night describe a second detail Palmes' own quoted testimony above doesn't spell out in this much length — that his blow aimed at Captain Preston (the one right after he struck the soldier) narrowly missed Preston's head and landed on his arm instead, by some accounts because Palmes slipped on the icy ground. A witness who was himself swinging a weapon in the final seconds before and after the first shot is describing his own actions, under oath, in a chaotic scene, about facts that bear directly on his own potential legal exposure. What would you check, knowing that, before taking his account of "who fired first" and "why" at face value? (There is no single settled answer here — historians and popular accounts genuinely disagree on some of the finer sequencing; naming that disagreement honestly is the correct move, not picking a version and stating it as fact.)

ss:L7.03:text:0:q3.text: Does the fact that Palmes physically struck a soldier make him an involved witness rather than a neutral one? Does that automatically make his account less trustworthy than a pure bystander's would be — or does it mean his stake and vantage point are different from Preston's, and need to be weighed on their own terms, the same as any other source?

ss:L7.03:text:1:0.text: Source 4 — from John Adams' closing argument for the defense, given at the soldiers' trial (December 1770), as recorded in the published trial transcript. Quoted directly, checked against the Founders Online Adams Papers transcription — see the precise source note below.

ss:L7.03:text:1:1.text: "Facts are stubborn things; and whatever may be our wishes, our inclinations, or the dictates of our passions, they cannot alter the state of facts and evidence."

ss:L7.03:text:1:q0.text: Who spoke this, when (relative to the trial's outcome), and for what purpose? Adams was a Patriot himself, arguing to acquit British soldiers — why might a Patriot lawyer choose this specific line as his argument's foundation?

ss:L7.03:text:1:q1.text: Given everything you now know from Sources 1–3 (a propaganda image, an accused officer's defense, and an involved witness's own testimony about his own actions), what do you think Adams meant by "facts... cannot alter the state of facts and evidence" — as a warning against which of the three sources' temptations specifically?

ss:L7.03:vocab:0.text: Discrepancy. a difference or disagreement between two accounts of the same thing. There was a discrepancy between the two witnesses' description of the getaway car's color.

ss:L7.03:vocab:1.text: Involved witness. a witness who was not just watching but did something during the event themselves (intervened, was struck, struck someone) — as distinct from a purely passive bystander. An involved witness is not automatically less honest, but their own actions can shape, understandably, how they remember and describe what happened next.

ss:L7.04:text:0:0.text: Headline: "Blue Light From Phones Wrecks Teen Sleep, New Study Finds"

ss:L7.04:text:0:1.text: A study released this month by a wellness startup, GlowGuard, claims that teenagers who use their phones in the hour before bed sleep dramatically worse than those who don't — and the company is using the finding to promote its blue-light-filtering phone case.

ss:L7.04:text:0:2.text: Researchers gave 24 volunteers, aged 15–17, from a single private school, a sleep-tracking wristband for one week. For the first three nights, participants used their phones normally before bed. For the next three nights, participants were asked to avoid phone screens for the hour before sleep. The wristbands measured total sleep time and how often each person woke up during the night.

ss:L7.04:text:0:3.text: On the "no phone" nights, the average participant fell asleep 9 minutes faster and had 1.2 fewer awakenings than on the "phone" nights. The company's press release states: "GlowGuard's research proves that screen time is the single biggest cause of poor sleep in teenagers today," and recommends its $34 phone case as "the scientifically-proven fix." The release does not mention whether participants were told which nights mattered to the study's hypothesis (which could have changed their behavior or self-reports), whether anything else about their evening routine changed between the two conditions, or whether the effect held for the group's typical teenager, given that all 24 participants attended the same private school and volunteered after seeing a flyer specifically about the study, which may itself attract families already concerned about screen time and sleep.

ss:L7.04:text:0:4.text: Outside the press release, a real body of published, peer-reviewed research on blue light, screens, and sleep does exist and does find some effect on falling-asleep time in larger, more carefully controlled studies — but the specific "wrecks" and "single biggest cause" language, the 24-person single-school sample, and the same company's product being sold as the "proven fix," are all reasons to read this particular article's own claim skeptically, even if the underlying general idea (screens before bed can affect sleep) has other, better support elsewhere.

ss:L7.04:vocab:1.text: Sample size. how many people, animals, or items were actually studied. A small sample can produce a dramatic-looking result by chance; a large sample is much harder to fool. a new study finds a new study of 14 college students over one weekend finds

ss:L7.04:vocab:2.text: Peer review. before serious scientific journals publish a study, other scientists in the field check the methodology for flaws. It doesn't make a study certainly true, but its absence (an unreviewed press release, a company's own blog post) is a warning sign.

ss:L7.05:text:0:1.text: Every summer, two numbers rise together in most countries with cold winters: ice cream sales and the number of people who drown. Track this across any year and the two lines climb and fall in almost the same shape, month by month. If you only looked at the correlation, you could write a headline: "Ice Cream Sales Linked to Drowning Deaths" — and it would be, strictly, true: the two numbers do correlate.

ss:L7.05:text:0:2.text: Nobody seriously believes ice cream causes drowning, or that drowning makes people crave ice cream. The real explanation is a confounding variable: hot weather. Hot weather makes people buy more ice cream, and hot weather also makes far more people go swimming — which is when almost all drownings happen. Ice cream and drowning are correlated only because they share a common cause; neither one causes the other at all.

ss:L7.05:text:0:3.text: This example is famous precisely because it's obvious once explained — which is exactly why it's useful. The same structure hides inside far less obvious, far more consequential claims: a study might find that people who take a particular vitamin have fewer heart attacks, and a headline might imply the vitamin protects the heart — when the real explanation could be that people who already exercise, don't smoke, and see a doctor regularly are more likely to take vitamins in the first place, and it's the exercise and non-smoking doing the protective work, not the pill.

ss:L7.06:text:0:0.text: Schools Should Ban Phones During the School Day — All Day, Not Just in Class

ss:L7.06:text:0:1.text: Last month, our district's school board considered banning phones only during class time, letting students use them freely at lunch and between periods. That policy doesn't go far enough. Schools should ban phones for the entire school day, and the case for doing so is stronger than most parents realize.

ss:L7.06:text:0:2.text: First, the evidence on attention is not close. A 2023 U.K. review of dozens of studies on phone use and student attention (cited by that country's Department for Education in its own guidance) found that even having a phone visible on a desk — turned off, screen down — measurably reduces performance on attention-demanding tasks, because part of the brain keeps tracking the phone's presence. A partial ban that allows phones at lunch means the phone is back in every student's pocket, and back on every student's mind, minutes before the next class starts.

ss:L7.06:text:0:3.text: Second, the case isn't only about attention in class — it's about what actually happens during unstructured time. Lunch and passing periods used to be when students practiced exactly the skills a phone lets them avoid: starting a conversation with someone new, sitting with discomfort instead of reaching for a screen, resolving a small disagreement face to face. Several districts that moved to all-day bans (not just in-class bans) reported, in follow-up surveys of teachers and staff, a rise in students eating lunch together in conversation rather than each alone on a phone — a change that a partial, in-class-only ban did not produce, because the phone was still available the moment class ended.

ss:L7.06:text:0:4.text: Opponents raise a real concern: parents want to be able to reach their child quickly in an emergency, and a full-day ban makes that harder. This is the strongest argument against an all-day policy, and it deserves a real answer, not dismissal. The answer most all-day-ban districts have used is a single, clearly communicated exception: the school office remains reachable by phone at all times, and in a genuine emergency, staff can reach any student in minutes — faster, in practice, than a parent could reach a distracted teenager glancing at a notification between classes. A full ban paired with a reliable office-contact system protects the one legitimate use case (real emergencies) without preserving the everyday use (texting friends at lunch) that the emergency argument was never really about.

ss:L7.06:text:0:5.text: A partial, in-class-only ban treats the problem as being about classroom instruction time alone. ss:L7.07:text:0:0.text: The Four-Day School Week Is Overdue

ss:L7.07:text:0:1.text: Districts nationwide are experimenting with four-day school weeks, and it's time more of them did. The case is straightforward, and the objections don't hold up under any real scrutiny.

ss:L7.07:text:0:2.text: Teachers everywhere are exhausted, and morale surveys from four-day districts consistently show higher teacher satisfaction and lower turnover than comparable five-day districts. A district superintendent in Colorado, who switched three years ago, put it simply: "Our teachers are happier and we're keeping more of them" — and honestly, if it's good enough for a superintendent who's actually run the experiment, that should settle the question for any parent still on the fence.

ss:L7.07:text:0:3.text: Critics say a four-day week hurts learning. But look at what's really being proposed here: some opponents act as though switching to four days means cutting a fifth of all instruction time entirely, as if the missing day simply vanishes into nothing — when in reality, most four-day districts extend the remaining four days by 45–60 minutes each, recovering most of the lost hours. The people attacking this policy the loudest, incidentally, tend to be the same superintendents who resisted remote learning changes during the pandemic and were proven wrong then too — so their objections here deserve the same skepticism.

ss:L7.07:text:0:4.text: And consider where this goes if we don't act: districts that refuse to modernize their schedules risk losing teachers to four-day neighbors first, then losing families who move district lines for a better schedule, and eventually risk collapsing entirely as enrollment drains away. The only real question left is whether your district moves now, while it can still choose the timing, or waits and has the decision forced on it later.

ss:L7.07:text:0:5.text: Either we adapt the school week to how families and teachers actually live today, or we keep pretending the traditional five-day model is untouchable — and given everything above, that's not really a choice at all.

ss:L7.10:text:0:0.text: A Full-Day Phone Ban Goes Too Far

ss:L7.10:text:0:1.text: Nobody disputes that phones distract students during class — the attention research on that point is genuinely strong, and no serious opponent of a full-day ban argues students should be texting during a lesson. The real disagreement is narrower than full-day-ban advocates suggest: should phones also be banned during lunch and passing periods, when class isn't happening at all?

ss:L7.10:text:0:2.text: A full-day ban treats a fifteen-year-old checking a message from a working parent, or coordinating a ride home, the same as a student ignoring a teacher mid-lesson — as if all phone use, everywhere in the building, is equally harmful. It isn't. The in-class case is about protecting instructional time from a specific, measurable distraction. The lunch-period case is about something much softer and less measurable: a hoped-for increase in face-to-face conversation, based on informal staff impressions in a handful of districts, not the kind of large, controlled research that backs the in-class case.

ss:L7.10:text:0:3.text: There's also a real equity dimension full-day-ban advocates rarely address directly: students who work part-time jobs, who care for younger siblings after school, or whose parents' work schedules are unpredictable, use lunchtime phone access to coordinate real logistics — a ride, a shift change, a sibling pickup — not just social messaging. A full ban's "office stays reachable" answer assumes every urgent need is an emergency the office would even know to relay; a text about a changed pickup time is not an emergency, but it's still something a student needs to handle, and an office switchboard is a poor substitute for a two-line text a student can send in ten seconds between classes.

ss:L7.10:text:0:4.text: None of this means "no phone policy at all." A ban on phone use during instructional time, strictly enforced, addresses the actual, well-evidenced problem. Extending that ban into every unstructured minute of the day trades a strong, specific case for a much weaker, more speculative one — and does it by treating every student's non-class phone use as equally disposable, which for some students, it simply isn't.

ss:L7.11:text:0:4.text: Context note: the standard five-day office week was itself a contested, gradually adopted change in the mid-20th century, resisted at first by many employers on exactly the same "productivity will suffer" grounds now used against hybrid/remote work — worth noting as historical pattern, not proof about today's specific question.

ss:L7.11:text:0:5.text: Source 3 — Science-style study summary (apply Session 4's claim/method/sample move)

ss:L7.11:text:0:6.text: A frequently cited 2015 workplace study (Bloom, Liang, Ouyang & Ying, published research on a Chinese travel-booking company) had customer-service employees volunteer to work from home for nine months, randomly assigning half to work from home and half to stay in the office —a real controlled experiment, not just an observed pattern. Home workers showed a 13% performance increase (more calls handled per shift), attributed mainly to a quieter environment and fewer sick days; however, home workers were also promoted at roughly half the rate of office workers over the same period, and after the experiment, many home workers voluntarily chose to return to the office, citing loneliness. This is a real, controlled, published, widely-cited study — but it studied one company, one job type (customer service), in one country, in 2015; whether its findings generalize to other kinds of work, or to today's post-pandemic environment, is a real, open question.

ss:L7.11:text:0:8.text: "The office isn't just a place to do tasks — it's where junior employees learn by watching how senior colleagues handle a hard client call, where a hallway conversation solves a problem that would have taken a week of scheduled video calls, and where a company's culture actually gets transmitted, not just described in a handbook. Every company that has fully abandoned the office is going to regret it within five years, when they realize they've raised a generation of employees who never learned the informal skills that only come from being physically present. Some hybrid advocates point to survey data showing employees prefer flexibility — but employee preference for an easier arrangement isn't the same as that arrangement being good for their long-term careers, any more than students preferring no homework means no homework is good for their education."

ss:L7.12:text:0:1.text: Mrs. Aldana kept a spare key to her daughter's apartment on a hook by the door, the way some people keep a fire extinguisher — a thing you own for an emergency you hope never comes, and check, now and then, just to be sure it's still there.

ss:L7.12:text:0:2.text: For eleven years the key hung untouched, gathering the particular dust of things nobody expects to need. Her daughter, Renata, called on Sundays, visited at Christmas, sent photographs of a life that looked, from the outside, entirely full — a husband, two children, a kitchen with a window over the sink where the light came in gold in the evenings. Mrs. Aldana kept the photographs on the refrigerator, a small gallery of a life she was allowed to watch but not, she understood, to enter uninvited.

ss:L7.12:text:0:3.text: Then, on a Tuesday in March, the telephone did not ring at its usual Sunday hour, and did not ring the Sunday after, and on the third silent Sunday Mrs. Aldana took the spare key down from its hook, feeling the strange lightness of a thing finally doing the job it had waited eleven years to do, and drove the four hours to her daughter's building with her heart performing something between a drumroll and a funeral march.

ss:L7.12:text:0:4.text: She let herself in expecting — she would later find it hard to say exactly what she had expected; her mind, in the car, had built entire wings of a house out of silence alone. What she found instead was her daughter at the kitchen table, very much alive, surrounded by paint swatches and takeout containers, in the middle of repainting the same golden kitchen a soft, deliberate blue, three weeks into a separation from her husband that she had not yet found the right sentence to explain over the phone.

ss:L7.12:text:0:5.text: "You still have the key," Renata said, not quite a question, looking at the small brass shape in her mother's hand as if it were a photograph of someone she used to be.

ss:L7.12:text:0:6.text: "I kept it on the hook by the door," Mrs. Aldana said. "I check that it's still there. I never thought I'd actually need to use it."

ss:L7.12:text:0:7.text: Renata almost laughed, the particular laugh of someone catching, for the first time, the shape of an old joke on herself. All those years, she had been the one performing a full life for the refrigerator gallery, careful to send only the golden-kitchen photographs and never the empty Tuesday evenings — and the one emergency the spare key had finally answered was not the catastrophe her mother's silence-built house had imagined, but her own quiet, unphotographed unraveling, three weeks along, that no phone call had yet found the courage to admit.

ss:L7.13:text:0:1.text: I want to be clear from the start that I am an extremely calm person, and that everything I did that Thursday was completely reasonable given the circumstances, and I would like whoever reads this to keep that firmly in mind, because I know how it's going to sound.

ss:L7.13:text:0:2.text: My neighbor, Mr. Feldt, had for several weeks been leaving his garbage bins out on the curb a full day early, which is, if you consult the homeowners' association bylaws — and I have, twice — a clear violation, and which I mentioned to him on four separate occasions, each time perfectly calmly, using a completely normal tone of voice that in no way could be described as anything but civil.

ss:L7.13:text:0:3.text: On the Thursday in question, I noticed the bins out again, a full eighteen hours early, and I want to stress that what I did next was not, as my wife later suggested, "unhinged" — that word is simply not accurate — but was, in fact, the only reasonable response left to a reasonable person who had already tried every reasonable channel. I moved the bins. That is all I did. I moved them, calmly, back onto his own driveway, which took, I will admit, several trips, since apparently four days' worth of garbage bins are heavier than one might expect, and I may have raised my voice slightly at one point when he came out onto his porch, though "screaming," which is the word his porch camera's audio apparently picked up according to the police officer who came by later — purely as a courtesy visit, nothing more — is, again, simply not an accurate description of a person who is completely calm.

ss:L7.13:text:0:4.text: The officer asked whether I thought this was, perhaps, an overreaction to a bylaw about garbage bins. I explained, calmly, that he clearly did not understand the full eighteen-day history of the situation, at which point he asked whether "eighteen days" sounded to me like something a calm person would have been counting. I did not think that question was especially relevant, and said so, calmly.

ss:L7.13:text:0:q0.text: List three specific phrases the narrator uses to insist they are "calm" or "reasonable." Why does a narrator who is genuinely calm rarely need to say so this many times?

ss:L7.13:text:0:q1.text: Think question: the narrator never once lies about a fact you can point to (the bins were moved; the officer did come by) — the unreliability is entirely in the interpretation laid on top of true events, not in the events themselves. Why can a narrator be unreliable while still technically telling the truth about every individual fact?

ss:L7.13:vocab:0.text: Unreliable narrator. a first-person narrator whose account the reader has reason to doubt — because they're lying, mistaken, mentally unwell, a child who doesn't understand what they're describing, or simply too invested in their own version of events to see it clearly. The reader has to read around the narrator's claims to reconstruct what's probably really true.

ss:L7.14:text:1:0.text: The Weight of a Decision You Didn't Notice Making

ss:L7.14:text:1:1.text: Most people, asked to name the biggest decision of their life, reach for the obvious candidates: a marriage, a career change, a move to a new city. Fewer people notice the decisions that were never really decided at all — the ones that accumulated, one unremarkable choice at a time, until a shape had formed that nobody had deliberately drawn.

ss:L7.14:text:1:2.text: Consider a habit as ordinary as checking a phone first thing in the morning. No one sits down and decides, formally, "I will now spend the first ninety seconds of every day absorbing whatever notification arrived overnight, before I have had a single unprompted thought of my own." And yet that is, in practice, the decision that gets made, daily, by the simple failure to make any decision at all — the phone is there, reaching for it costs nothing in the moment, and the accumulated cost only becomes visible zoomed out, across a year, in a way no single morning ever reveals.

ss:L7.14:text:1:3.text: Behavioral researchers have a name for the gap this exploits: present bias — the well- documented tendency to weigh a cost or benefit happening right now far more heavily than an identical cost or benefit happening later, even when, calculated honestly, the two should carry equal weight. Present bias is not a character flaw unique to distracted people; it is close to a universal feature of how human decision-making works, which is exactly why it is so effectively exploited, deliberately, by the design of anything competing for attention — a notification is engineered to make "later" (finishing the thought you were having, sleeping fully) lose to "now" (checking) every single time the two compete, because the app's success is measured by exactly how often "now" wins.

ss:L7.14:text:1:4.text: None of this means the fix is willpower, applied harder, in the moment of temptation — present bias, by definition, is precisely the bias that makes in-the-moment willpower an unreliable defense, since the moment itself is engineered to feel low-stakes. The more durable fix, according to the same research tradition, is structural: decisions made in advance, at a calm moment, that remove the in-the-moment choice altogether — a phone charging outside the bedroom, not a phone charging on the nightstand with a promise not to check it; a specific, scheduled time for messages, not an open-ended "I'll just glance quickly" available at every idle moment. The insight generalizes well past phones: nearly any habit someone describes as a failure of willpower is, on closer inspection, better described as a structural decision that was never made — an environment left to default toward whatever is easiest in the moment, which is rarely the same as whatever the person, asked calmly in advance, would actually choose.

ss:L7.14:text:1:5.text: This is, in its own way, exactly the disciplinary-reading lesson this level has spent thirteen sessions building toward, aimed inward instead of outward: the same habit of asking "what's actually driving this outcome — the obvious surface reason, or something structural and less visible underneath it" that a historian applies to a deposition, a scientist applies to a correlation, and a critical reader applies to a headline, applies with equal force to a person's own daily habits, if they're willing to read their own life with the same disciplined skepticism they've just spent this level learning to apply to everyone else's claims.

ss:L7.14:vocab:0.text: Skim. moving quickly over a whole text to get the general shape/gist (what's this about, roughly, and is it worth reading closely?) — not aiming to catch every detail.

ss:L7.14:vocab:1.text: Scan. moving quickly through a text looking for one specific piece of information (a date, a name, a number) — not reading for overall meaning at all.

ss:L7.14:vocab:2.text: Deep reading. slow, careful, often reread reading, aimed at full comprehension of a dense or important passage — the mode this whole level has mostly used.

t2:L3.01:0.text: urgent. Urgent means something urgent needs attention right away, it can't wait.

t2:L3.02:0.text: rough. Rough means not smooth; bumpy or hard to deal with.

t2:L3.03:0.text: reliable. Reliable means something or someone you can count on, again and again.

t2:L3.04:0.text: routine. Routine means a set of steps you do the same way, again and again.

t2:L3.05:0.text: precise. Precise means exact, with no room for error.

t2:L3.06:0.text: gratitude. Gratitude means a strong feeling of thanks for something someone did.

t2:L3.07:0.text: minor. Minor means small, not serious.

t2:L3.08:0.text: economy. Economy means the way money and goods move around in a place — who earns it, who spends it, who it helps.

t2:L3.09:0.text: domesticated. Domesticated means tamed and cared for by people, instead of living wild.

t2:L3.10:0.text: temporary. Temporary means lasting only for a short time, not permanent.

t2:L3.11:0.text: responsibility. Responsibility means a duty or job that is yours to take care of.

t2:L3.12:0.text: noticeably. Noticeably means in a way you can clearly see or notice.

t2:L3.13:0.text: perspective. Perspective means a way of looking at or thinking about something.

t2:L3.14:0.text: confident. Confident means sure of yourself, believing you can do something well.

t2:L3.15:0.text: absorbing. Absorbing means so interesting that it holds your full attention.

t2:L3.16:0.text: daunting. Daunting means something that feels big and a bit scary to start.

t2:L3.17:0.text: fulfillment. Fulfillment means a deep feeling of satisfaction from doing something meaningful.

t2:L4.01:0.text: constellation. Constellation means a group of stars that makes a shape people gave a name to, like a picture in the sky.

t2:L4.02:0.text: caravan. Caravan means a group of people traveling together, usually a long way, for safety and company.

t2:L4.03:0.text: calling. Calling means a job or purpose a person feels strongly drawn to, more than just work for money.

t2:L4.04:0.text: cautious. Cautious means careful, watching closely for danger before acting.

t2:L4.05:0.text: harmonious. Harmonious means peaceful and working well together, without fighting or friction.

t2:L4.06:0.text: resilience. Resilience means the ability to recover from something hard and keep going.

t2:L4.07:0.text: composed. Composed means calm and in control, not panicked, even in a stressful moment.

t2:L4.08:0.text: composure. Composure means staying calm and thinking clearly, even when something unexpected or painful happens.

t2:L4.09:0.text: compassion. Compassion means caring deeply about someone else's suffering and wanting to help.

t2:L4.10:0.text: diligence. Diligence means careful, steady effort, especially in checking details before finishing a job.

t2:L4.11:0.text: attentiveness. Attentiveness means paying close, careful attention to someone or something, noticing details.

t2:L4.12:0.text: folklore. Folklore means traditional stories, beliefs, and sayings passed down through a community, often about nature or luck.

t2:L4.13:0.text: perseverance. Perseverance means continuing to try, even when something is hard or takes a long time.

t2:L4.14:0.text: troubleshooting. Troubleshooting means solving a problem by checking possible causes one at a time, in order, instead of guessing.

t2:L4.15:0.text: functional. Functional means designed to do a practical job, not just to entertain or tell a story.
